blocks.text: Chapter 40. Practicing the Way Lies in the Mind

inline.s: The Buddha said: In walking the Way, a renunciant should not be like the ox at the mill — though the body plods the path, the mind within does not. If the mind walks the Way, what need is there to move the body?
A renunciant walking the Way should not be like the ox that turns the mill: though the body treads the path, the mind has not. If the mind walks the Way, what need is there for the body to walk it?
Therefore, in practice the precious thing is to cultivate the mind; walking the Way lies in the mind, not in the outward form.

If the mind walks the Way, what need to move the body?” This is spoken for those who are “without thought, without abiding, without practice, without attainment.” If one has not yet reached the emptiness of both mind and states, then let the practice of the mind take the lead, body and mind advancing together. To take the correcting of faults as an example: there is correction by affairs, correction by principle, and correction by mind. On the relation and use of these three, Liao-Fan’s Four Lessons says: “On the whole, what is most excellent corrects the mind, and purity arises on the spot; the moment a thought stirs it is perceived, and being perceived it vanishes. If one cannot yet do this, one must comprehend principle so as to dispel it; and if still one cannot, one must restrain it together with the affair at hand. To practice the higher work while still carrying out the lower is no strategy at fault; but to cling to the lower and be blind to the higher is clumsy indeed.”

blocks.text: Chapter 41. An Upright Mind Escapes Desire

inline.s: The Buddha said: One who practices the Way is like an ox laden with a heavy load, trudging through deep mire — utterly spent, not daring to glance left or right, until he comes out of the mud and may at last rest. So too a renunciant should see that passion and desire are more perilous than mud, and, with an upright mind, think only of the Way, and so be free of suffering.

The practicer of the Way is like an ox burdened and walking through deep mud: though utterly exhausted, he dares not relax in the least — he will not even glance left or right until he has left the mire, and only then may he stop and take his rest. A renunciant should see that the peril of passion and desire is greater than that of mud, and only by fixing his whole mind on the Way, his eyes never turning aside, going bravely forward, can he emerge from desire and so be freed from suffering!
[suxi] To rest; to stop and catch one’s breath.

blocks.text: Chapter 42. All Dharmas Are Like an Illusion

inline.s: The Buddha said: I look upon the throne of kings and princes as upon grains of dust through a crevice. I look upon treasures of gold and jade as upon broken tiles. I look upon robes of finest white silk as upon tattered cloth. I look upon the great thousand-world as upon a single myrobalan. I look upon the waters of Lake Anavatapta as upon the oil used to anoint the feet. I look upon the gates of expedient means as upon a heap of conjured jewels. I look upon the supreme vehicle as upon gold and silk in a dream. I look upon the Way of the Buddha as upon flowers before the eyes. I look upon meditative absorption as upon Mount Sumeru standing firm. I look upon nirvana as upon awaking from a day-and-night slumber. I look upon the inverted and the upright as upon the dance of six dragons. I look upon equality as upon the one true ground. I look upon the flourishing guidance of beings as upon the trees of the four seasons.

I regard the rank of kings and princes as dust drifting through a crevice. I regard the treasures of gold and jade as broken tiles. I regard robes of pure white silk as rotten rags. I regard the great thousand-world as a single myrobalan (the chebula fruit, wrinkled like an olive). I regard the waters of Lake Anavatapta as the oil for anointing the feet. I regard the many gates of expedient means as a heap of conjured jewels. I regard the supreme vehicle as the gold and silver of a dream. I regard the Way of the Buddha as empty flowers before the eyes. I regard meditative absorption as Mount Sumeru, towering immovably. I regard nirvana as a man awaking from sleep. I regard the inverted and the upright as the dance of six dragons (a figure for the six faculties), head and tail merely exchanging place. I regard equality as the real ground of the one true realm. I regard the flourishing guidance of beings by the Dharma as the trees of the four seasons: budding in spring, luxuriant in summer, bearing fruit in autumn, dropping leaves in winter, in endless cycle.
Set at the close of the sutra, this chapter reveals the Buddha’s eye of equality beholding all things alike, in order to destroy beings’ clinging to dharmas.

[Clinging to dharmas] To cling wrongly to dharmas as real. The Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, illusory and without reality, having no root.” (The Sutra of Sustaining the World) [Dust through a crevice] Dust passing through a narrow crack — a figure for what is utterly trifling and fleeting, like a mote drifting before a tiny opening. [Broken tiles] Fragments of brick and stone. [Fine white silk] Exquisite, spotless white silk. [Tattered cloth] Worn-out, torn rags.

[Great thousand-world] That is, the great chiliocosm. One great thousand-world is the region in which a single Buddha teaches. Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents forms one small world; a thousand such small worlds form one small thousand-world; a thousand small thousand-worlds form one middle thousand-world; a thousand middle thousand-worlds form one great thousand-world. Since it is counted in thousands three times over, one great thousand-world is also called the “three-thousand great thousand-world.” [Mount Sumeru] Rendered in Chinese as “the lofty and wonderful mountain”; it is the center of one small world. This mountain is made of the four jewels — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Its form is broad above and broad below but narrow in the middle, exceeding tall and exceeding great, beyond comparison with any other mountain, the king of mountains. [Four great continents] About Mount Sumeru lie four great continents: in the east, East Videha; in the south, Jambudvipa (the world in which we dwell is on this continent); in the west, Godaniya; in the north, Uttarakuru. [Myrobalan] That is, the chebula fruit. The Compendium of Materia Medica says: “The Terminalia chebula tree is like the cork-tree; its flowers are white, its fruit like gardenia. Chiefly it disperses phlegm and sends the qi downward. It arrives on ships from beyond the southern seas, and is also found in Guangzhou.”

[Regarding the waters of Lake Anavatapta as like the oil for anointing the feet] To regard the dear waters of Lake Anavatapta as the cheap oil with which one anoints the feet — between them no difference at all. [Lake Anavatapta] That is, Lake Anavatapta, called “the lake without heat and vexation,” some eight hundred li in circuit. Its banks are adorned with the four jewels — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and “beautiful crystal” (answering to this world’s crystal, which bears the four tints of purple, white, red, and green). Its bed is spread with golden sand, and its clear waves mirror like burnished glass. [Regarding the supreme vehicle as like the gold and silk of a dream] To regard the supreme vehicle as but the gold and silk seen in a dream. [Gold and silk] Gold and fine silk — in general, money and precious things. [Supreme vehicle] The Dharma of the utmost preeminence. Master Ouyi says: “Though the supreme vehicle is said to be the most real, yet it is all the principle inherent in the nature of sentient beings; outside the mind there is no Dharma. Hence it is said: perfect enlightenment returns to having nothing attained. Like the gold and silk of a dream — how could any real thing be gotten from it?”

[Regarding the Way of the Buddha as like flowers before the eyes] The many forms of the Buddha’s Way are set up to counter the deluded mind; if the deluded mind does not arise, how can there be any Way of the Buddha? The saying runs: “Unconditioned, neither arising nor ceasing, unreal as flowers in the sky.” [Flowers in the sky] Flowers in the open sky (the ancient word for blossom being the same as that for flower); a figure for illusion. One with a diseased eye sees flowers in the sky, yet in the sky there are no flowers at all — only the wrong perception of a diseased eye. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Mistakenly taking the four elements for one’s own body and the reflected images of the six dusts for the mark of one’s own mind — like the diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon.”

[Regarding meditative absorption as like the pillar of Sumeru] Sumeru rises from the sea and wind and wave cannot move it; so too absorption holds the mind, and states and perceptions cannot sway it. Yet Sumeru is illusory, and absorption is illusory as well. [Pillar of Sumeru] That is, Mount Sumeru; the word “pillar” describes that mountain’s immeasurable mass, answering to the earlier “I look upon the great thousand-world as a single myrobalan.” [Regarding nirvana as like awaking from a day-and-night slumber] Birth and death are as a long night, bound by ignorance, so by day and by night all are asleep; nirvana is as the everlasting day, with wisdom opened wide, so by day and by night all are awake. [Regarding the inverted and the upright as like the dance of six dragons] In wheeling through birth and death there is only the six faculties; in the peace of nirvana there is also only the six faculties. To turn away from enlightenment and mingle with the dusts is called “inverted,” yet in truth there is no decrease; to turn away from the dusts and join with enlightenment is called “upright,” yet in truth there is no increase. Hence it is but like the dance of six dragons (a figure for the six faculties), head and tail merely exchanging places — nothing more.

[Regarding equality as like the one true ground] To regard all dharmas as equal is like the one true ground. [One true ground] The real ground realized in the awakening to the one true realm. [One true realm] The single real dharma-realm, the only true realm — that is, the realm of the Buddha. The dharmakaya, equal for all Buddhas, from the very beginning neither arising nor ceasing, neither existing nor empty, beyond name and beyond mark, without within and without without, solely real and inconceivable — this is called “the one true realm.”
